topic: The Magic of Averages: Understanding the Central Limit Theorem
target_audience: University students or introductory data science learners

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Individual vs. The Average
lecture_lines: Every population has a mean, labeled mu.
Standard deviation, sigma, measures the spread.
Individual data points are often messy and unpredictable.
Let's look at heights in a giraffe forest.
This raw distribution is chaotic and skewed.
animations: Create a horizontal axis (#FFFFFF) and scatter 100 circles (#ADD8E6) to represent a messy giraffe population.
Draw a highly skewed, non-normal distribution curve (#FFA500) over the points.
Add a bold vertical line at the mean position with label 'μ' in color #FFFFFF.
Highlight several individual circles by changing their color to #FFD700 to show 'unpredictability'.
Shift the entire set of points and curve to the top half of the screen.

sections.title: The Sampling Experiment
lecture_lines: First, we select a random sample of thirty giraffes.
Next, we calculate the average height for this group.
This average becomes a single dot on our graph.
We repeat this process multiple times to gather data.
Watch as a thousand sample averages rain down below.
animations: Highlight 30 random circles in the top population by changing their color to #00FF00.
Display the text 'Sample size: n = 30' (#FFD700) above the highlighted circles.
Animate the 30 green circles moving to the center and merging into one yellow dot (#FFFF00).
Drop the yellow dot onto the bottom horizontal axis (#FFFFFF).
Generate a 'rain' of 1,000 yellow dots (#FFFF00) falling and stacking on the bottom axis.

sections.title: The Transformation (The 'Magic' Moment)
lecture_lines: We repeat this sampling process many, many times.
Watch as thousands of sample averages are plotted.
A specific shape begins to emerge from the chaos.
Despite the messy start, we see a bell curve.
This is the magic of the sampling distribution.
animations: As dots stack on the bottom axis, they begin forming a bell shape.
Fade out individual yellow dots and replace them with a smooth bell curve (#FFFFFF).
Draw a vertical line of symmetry (#00FFFF) labeled 'Mean of Averages'.
Flash the original messy curve (#FFA500) and the new bell curve (#FFFFFF) side-by-side.
Add a glowing label 'Normal Distribution' (#FFD700) next to the bell curve.

sections.title: The Core Rules of CLT
lecture_lines: The curve's center matches the true population mean.
Larger samples create a narrower, more precise curve.
Usually, thirty or more samples ensure this symmetry.
animations: Show the population 'μ' and the bell curve's center aligning via a dashed line (#FFFFFF).
Simultaneously display a wide bell curve (#FF6347, n=5) and a narrow one (#32CD32, n=50).
Display the text 'Magic Threshold: n ≥ 30' in bold gold (#FFD700) at the center.

sections.title: Why It Matters: Real-World Application
lecture_lines: CLT helps us predict behavior in complex systems.
Imagine a factory making bars of varying weights.
Averages help managers ensure consistent quality control.
animations: Display 5 'Chocolate Bar' rectangles (#A52A2A) moving on a conveyor belt.
Group 40 bars and show their average weight falling onto a narrow bell curve.
Highlight a 'Failure Zone' at the tails of the bell curve in #FF0000.

sections.title: Summary & Conclusion
lecture_lines: We moved from messy data to orderly curves.
The CLT is the bridge to powerful statistics.
Understand the average to master the whole.
